title: Learning Knowledge - 1
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Opening a mini-series comparing knowledge, skills and understanding, Skelton argues they are learned, taught and assessed differently. He begins with knowledge, defined as factual information, and lists eight shared characteristics. Knowledge is broadly agreed to be true, foundational, continually expanding, assessed as right or wrong, often learned out of context, relatively impersonal, acquired mainly by being told, and recalled with hooks. Examples range from quiz shows and fake election claims to his mother-in-law's memory and music mnemonics. He explains that this framework will later help show why different kinds of learning demand different teaching and assessment.
points: Knowledge, skills and understanding are learned, taught and assessed differently, and recognising this saves confusion.
Factual knowledge is defined by general agreement that the evidence supports it, which is why fake facts can arise within sub-groups.
Because knowledge keeps expanding, curriculum designers must choose what to hardwire.
Knowledge's right/wrong nature makes it quick and cheap to test, which explains why school assessment leans on it.
Facts are often learned without any experience of the thing itself, and are recalled through hooks and mnemonics.
quotes: Statements become factual knowledge when the evidence base for each is accepted as valid and there is general agreement that they are ‘true’.

Every subject, every discipline and every thought we have has at its foundational base a collection of particularly relevant facts. Factual knowledge matters. The debate, as we shall see later, is about how much matters and when it matters.

This incessant depositing of new knowledge on top of old knowledge means that curriculum writers, schools and others have to decide what repeatedly experienced knowledge we - including children and students - should hardwire. We can’t hardwire it all.

That’s why in schools, judging whether children have learned the required knowledge is always about testing and why knowledge testing is so common. Testing knowledge is quick, relatively easy to mark, cheap and applicable to almost everyone.
In other words, we can win quizzes and pass school tests by knowing things of which we have no real experience at all. Which is what many quiz winners do all the time.

As pieces of knowledge flow like grains of sand on to an ever-growing pile, recovering one grain can be difficult. Memory wizards, those people who can remember the names of 25 playing cards they have just seen in random order, have all sorts of tricks - there are lots of them - to help them isolate the grains of factual knowledge they need.
